title: What If We Detonated All Nuclear Bombs at Once?
beats: Viewers asked: explode every nuclear weapon at once? Mock-serious, scientists were gathered to calculate
Sets the quantity: 15,000 weapons, split by country
Translate into cities: 4,500 big cities at about 3 bombs each, so half of humanity could die and 1,500 bombs remain: 'overkill'
Make the pile: all 15,000 fit in one warehouse, dropped in the Amazon
3 billion tons TNT as stacked TNT rebuilding Manhattan; compared with Krakatoa, 15x its energy
Countdown; fireball, blast area, fires, shock wave circling Earth, crater
Fallout and nuclear winter: bad regionally, humanity survives
'OK, but what if we explode more': escalate
Mine all uranium: pile of 10 billion Hiroshimas, 3 km cube, equal to the dinosaur asteroid energy
Second countdown; ground splashes like water, 100 km crater, ejecta to space, global quakes, firestorms
Ash blocks sun, near freezing, decades of winter, extinction of large animals including humans
Survivors in bunkers and subs, ISS destroyed, wasteland
Planet heals in million years; future intelligent life finds a thin radioactive layer and is confused

metrics.misconception: partial: assumes 15,000 bombs ends humanity; answer is no, Amazon dies but humans continue (3:49)
metrics.brute_force: yes 0:35: just count bombs times cities, then pile everything
metrics.examples: 2 pile scenarios, escalating roughly 15,000 warheads to uranium-limit; each repeats the template: size, countdown, blast, fire, fallout, climate
metrics.ending: Dark-humor epilogue of future beings finding the strata, callback to the question's absurd premise

principles.1: confirmed: city counts and Manhattan/Krakatoa comparisons at 0:35-2:07 convert abstract tonnage to familiar things
principles.2: confirmed: only unit shift is TNT to Hiroshima bombs (4:24); no formulas
principles.4: partly: analogies for scale (TNT Manhattan, Krakatoa, dinosaur asteroid) but no rigor step
principles.5: confirmed: 'push the button, three two one' at 2:27 and 4:40 acts out the scenario literally, in second person
principles.6: confirmed: crude city-by-bomb multiplication at 0:57 comes before the pile
principles.7: partly: the escalation invites viewer to see the threshold between 'bad' and 'extinction' but stated as narration
principles.8: partly: speech flat; idea rate is higher during the first scenario and lower in the second narrative; no detectable slowdown for novel concepts
principles.9: confirmed: both explosions repeat the same sequence of effects, making the escalation visible (2:27 vs 4:40)
principles.10: confirmed: country counts to cities to one pile to a larger pile
principles.11: confirmed: count, per-city effect, one pile, bigger pile, aftermath in order
principles.12: confirmed: Krakatoa, dinosaur asteroid, Hiroshima, geology 'thin layer' tie to real events
principles.13: partly: playful but concrete; expert-depth reasoning like why 3 bombs per city is only assumed at 0:57

new_moves.name: escalate-the-what-if
new_moves.what: Run the same scenario at one order of magnitude greater, using the first run as baseline so each effect gets a comparison

new_moves.name: scale-to-familiar-object
new_moves.what: Convert unimaginable energy to a physical object a viewer can picture (Manhattan built from TNT, warehouse pile)

new_moves.name: cosmic-indifference-coda
new_moves.what: End by zooming out to the planet and aliens/future life reading the evidence

theory: The video uses a counterfactual toy world and a literal countdown, then repeats the same effect-sequence at a bigger magnitude. The repeated template lets the viewer feel the threshold between disaster and extinction without equations. Comedy and familiar anchors (Manhattan, Krakatoa) keep dread tolerable.
velocity: Scene builder: a 'what-if slider' scene that reruns one effect template at 1x, 100x, 10,000x energy
Voice: dark-humor and countdown cadence are a pacing tool; allow orchestrator a 'beat of silence' before the reveal
Orchestrator playbook 'counterfactual escalation': baseline, comparison anchor, escalate, aftermath
Learner model: ask learner to guess outcome before the second run, using the first as evidence
Evals: check that every scale number gets a familiar anchor within one beat
quote: Now that's what an expert would call, overkill.
